title: Gold, weapons or a 'Rosetta stone': Which archaeological treasure would you most like to discover?
summary: From ancient coins to long-lost texts, archaeologists uncovered countless artifacts for centuries. Live Science asks its readers which one they'd want to discover themselves.
content: Archaeological discoveries can offer remarkable insights into the lives, cultures and beliefs of ancient peoples. From richly furnished royal tombs to caches of silver coins , some of the most significant finds have revealed how people lived, traded, fought , governed and died thousands of years ago. Related stories 'Links with the British royal family would eventually prove crucial': How DNA solved the 70-year mystery of what happened to the executed members of the last Russian imperial family Ghostly 'sand body' double burial unearthed at Sutton Hoo 2,600-year-old inscription in Turkey finally deciphered — and it mentions goddess known 'simply as the Mother' Other discoveries stand out for their extraordinary preservation or historical significance. For example, the most expensive shipwreck on record — the 300-year-old Spanish galleon San José that's worth an estimated $17 billion — was found off the coast of Colombia in 2015 and continues to inform archaeologists and challenge governments that can't agree about its modern ownership. Meanwhile, ancient texts can provide invaluable clues about long-lost languages and civilizations. The Rosetta stone opened up the world of ancient Egypt to scholars, but researchers are still trying to decipher the mysterious Indus Valley script , one of the world's earliest urban civilizations. Each type of discovery offers a new window to the ancient world. But which of these archaeological treasures would you most want to uncover? title: Hoxne 'Empress' pepper pot: A 1,600-year-old silver and gold pepper shaker that a UK farmer unearthed while looking for his hammer
summary: This silver pepper shaker reveals the Romans' love of the spice and the lengths they would go to procure it.
content: The pepper shaker was discovered as part of an ancient Roman hoard. (Image credit: Alamy) QUICK FACTS Name: Hoxne 'Empress' pepper pot What it is: A silver spice dispenser Where it is from: Hoxne, Suffolk, England When it was made: A.D. 350 to 400 In 1992, a farmer in the village of Hoxne in southeastern England was searching for a lost hammer with a metal detector when he stumbled upon a massive hoard of more than 15,000 ancient Roman coins, jewelry and tableware. Among the artifacts in the Hoxne hoard was a silver spice container in the shape of an imperial lady. The artifact, named the Empress, is one of four pepper pots ("piperatoria" in Latin) discovered in the Hoxne hoard, according to the British Museum . The silver container stands about 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is decorated with gold around the woman's eyes, mouth, hair and accessories, including a scroll in her left hand. The woman's elaborate hairstyle helps date the creation of the pepper pot to the fourth century, but experts think the hoard may have been buried in the early fifth century, when Roman rule in Britain was ending. At the bottom of the pot, which rests on a four-legged base, there is a disc that can be set at three positions: wide open, closed and partly open. The pot would have been filled in the open position with cracked pepper and then used in the partly open position for sprinkling the spice over food. The ancient Romans were huge fans of pepper, Neil MacGregor, former director of the British Museum, wrote in " A History of the World in 100 Objects " (Penguin Books, 2010). Pepper didn't grow in the Roman Empire , so merchants procured it from India. This made it an expensive spice, and filling up the pepper pot would have been costly. A wealthy Romano-British family likely used the pepper pot as elaborate tableware, MacGregor wrote. It is unclear whom the Empress was meant to depict, but researchers don't think it features a member of the Roman imperial family. However, the fact that she holds a scroll could indicate that she was both wealthy and well educated. The ancient family who lived near Hoxne seems to have left its wealth behind during the breakdown of Roman rule in Britain, since the pepper pot was found in a chest that contained dozens of pieces of silverware, 29 pieces of gold jewelry, and more than 15,000 coins. "This was the mobile wealth of a rich Roman family — precisely the type of person who is in danger when the state fails," MacGregor wrote. For more stunning archaeological discoveries, check out our Astonishing Artifacts archives. Etruscan Abecedarium Lycurgus Cup Mold Gold Cape Can you put together last week's Astonishing Artifact ?

title: Impossible volcanic eruption spotted in deepest part of the ocean, perplexing scientists
summary: Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.
content: A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity. This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern , a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery. Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79. "It's not something that as a geoscientist I would have said would be predicted," said Sune Nielsen , a geochemist at the University of Lorraine in France who was not involved in the study. "Very far from it." A fish in the genus Pseudoliparis in an image taken during during a dive by the Jason/Medea ROV at 20,659 feet (6,297 m). (Image credit: Image by Dr. Tomoyo Okumura, taken as part of Cruise TN438, supported by the National Science Foundation) The deepest place on Earth The Challenger Deep is in the remote western Pacific at the southern end of the Mariana Trench. There, the Pacific oceanic plate pushes under the Mariana oceanic plate in a process called subduction . At the trench where the two plates meet, the ocean floor plunges down 6.8 miles (10.9 kilometers). Mount Everest could fit in the chasm, with room to spare. Geoscientists aren't sure why the trench is so dizzyingly deep, but they have turned up some clues. For instance, there is a tear in the Pacific Plate that allows one narrow strip of the plate to subduct particularly rapidly. The curvature of the plate is also very steep, perhaps because the rocks of the Mariana and Pacific plates aren't very strongly connected to each other, allowing the Pacific Plate to dive steeply and flex freely. The new findings, reported Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science , suggest that volcanism and magma also may play a role, Stern said. The researchers were exploring a segment of the Challenger Deep's forearc, a roughly 120-mile-wide (200 km) expanse that sits between the trench itself and the volcanic arc created by the subduction zone. These volcanic arcs are standard subduction zone features; for example, Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier are part of the volcanic arc of the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest. But though there are some volcanoes north of Challenger Deep along the Mariana Trench, the Challenger Deep segment of the trench is odd in that there is not an organized volcanic arc there. Instead, there's an ocean ridge. Regardless, the space between this ridge and the trench was expected to be volcanically quiet because there is not usually enough heat in that region of a subduction zone to melt magma. Nevertheless, the cameras on the deep-diving remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea, which went to the site in 2014, caught strange, pancake-like rock features at three different spots in a 60-mile (100 km) stretch of the trench. Samples brought on board the ship revealed rock embedded with volcanic glass and a pyroclastic flow texture. A sea cucumber in an image from the Jason/Medea dive at 12,726 feet (3879 m). (Image credit: Image by Dr. Tomoyo Okumura, taken as part of Cruise TN438, supported by the National Science Foundation) New mysteries The researchers are currently getting the rock dated, but volcanic glass usually erodes quickly in the ocean, Stern said, so the presence of glass suggests the eruptions were fairly recent. "They're not yesterday," he said, "but I don't think they're a million years old." The pressure of the water at the depths of the flows is equivalent to 592 atmospheres of Earth stacked on top of one another. Typically, that kind of pressure keeps a lid on the dissolved water and carbon dioxide in magma that expands rapidly to cause explosive eruptions. Thus, Stern said, the eruptions by the Challenger Deep may have been driven by a supercritical fluid ‪—‬ a weird state sort of in between a gas and a liquid. "We just don’t know how those magmas will behave at those water depths," said Stephen Self , a volcanologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the study. The mission's observations also suggest that the crust of this region is extending, or stretching, in two different ways. To the east, the stretch is caused by a mechanical pulling apart of the crust. To the west, volcanic eruptions are stretching the crust. It's a perplexing finding, Nielsen said, without a clear explanation. Related stories Eruptions of ocean volcanoes may be the echoes of ancient continental breakups Tectonic plates can spread subduction like a contagion An ocean of magma formed early in Earth's history, and it may still influence our planet today, study finds Stern and his colleagues suspect that the two plates are starting a new subduction zone in this western part. That would be an exciting finding; subduction zones move around over tens of millions of years, and researchers don't know much about how new ones start. The geochemical studies of the rocks that Stern and his team pulled up could answer questions about where the lava that made the pyroclastic flows came from and why this bizarre region can generate magma where none should be. "This region is really, really unusual for our planet, and there is quite a bit of, 'What, really? Wait, how is that? OK, yeah, I guess maybe.'" Nielsen said. "So obviously, I find it super interesting." What do you know about the deepest place on Earth? Find out with our Mariana Trench quiz!

title: BepiColombo ends 8-year interplanetary journey to Mercury. What's next for the ambitious spacecraft?
summary: The BepiColombo spacecraft has overcome a last-minute computer glitch to enter orbit around Mercury — the 2nd craft in history to orbit the closest planet to the sun.
content: Update: On Tuesday (Nov. 24) ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher announced on X that the BepiColombo team has isolated the computer glitch, and tweaked the mission accordingly. "The remaining manoeuvres have already been replanned, with no extra burns needed," Aschbacher said. The two probes are still on track to seprate on Dec. 9. (This article was updated at 11:40 a.m. ET on Nov. 24). After eight years slingshotting around the inner solar system, the joint European-Japanese spacecraft BepiColombo has finally entered into orbit around Mercury — becoming only the second mission ever to orbit the closest planet to the sun. Mission scientists confirmed on Saturday (Nov. 21) that the spacecraft reached Mercury's orbit and is transmitting data back to the ground team. However, the orbital insertion didn't go entirely as planned, European Space Agency (ESA) representatives said in a statement on Monday. Due to a software glitch, the spacecraft didn't fire its thrusters for the full 37 minutes required to slow its approach to Mercury. ESA has investigates the issue and confirmed the spacecraft's new trajectory; meanwhile, BepiColombo remains "safe," the statement noted. The spacecraft should be ready to begin a year of intensive science observations of Mercury starting a few months from now. An illustration of BepiColombo approaching Mercury for orbital insertion. (Image credit: ESA) BepiColombo's space odyssey Built jointly by ESA and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), BepiColombo is actually two separate probes, which are currently stacked one atop the other in orbit. The ESA-built orbiter, named the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), and the JAXA-built orbiter, the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), carry separate science instruments, and they will soon diverge into separate orbital paths around the mysterious inner planet, operating as two probes gathering different streams of data. A selfie of BepiColombo during a flyby of Mercury's north pole in 2025. (Image credit: ESA) The pair of probes launched together aboard an Ariane 5 rocket in October 2018, and spent the following eight years on an interplanetary journey that took them past Earth, the moon and Venus. It even passed by Mercury itself six times. (During one of these flybys, in January 2025, Bepi snapped an incredible closeup photo of Mercury's north pole .) This complicated cosmic choreography was necessary to prevent BepiColombo from picking up too much speed and overshooting Mercury's orbit, according to ESA. Mercury sits about 36 million miles (58 million kilometers) from our star, or roughly one third of the distance between Earth and the sun. That makes it very difficult for a spacecraft to reach Mercury without being captured by the sun's considerable gravitational pull and dragged off course. Only one other spacecraft — NASA's MESSENGER probe — has succeeded in entering Mercury orbit before, circling the planet from 2011 to 2015 after its own seven-year journey through space. What will BepiColombo study now? BepiColombo will spend the next few months getting both probes in position to start mapping Mercury in the greatest detail ever. MPO and Mio are expected to separate in early December, with Mio entering a highly elliptical orbit around Mercury's poles. MPO will then take a few more months to fine-tune its trajectory, reaching a lower and more circular polar orbit in March 2027, according to ESA . Its science operations are expected to begin in April. Related stories Mercury may have shrunk much more than we thought, new study hints Mercury is weird because of a 'hit-and-run' incident in its youth Mercury's 'missing' meteorites may have finally been found on Earth The sibling probes will each orbit Mercury several times a day, with MPO completing an orbit every 2 hours or so . Observing the mysterious inner planet from several different vantage points, the probes will make the most comprehensive map of Mercury ever. The mission's suite of science instruments will study the planet across the electromagnetic spectrum , taking observations in X-rays, gamma-rays and ultraviolet light, as well as collecting detailed measurements of the planet's magnetic field. With this information, scientists hope to unravel many mysteries of the least-explored planet in the solar system. The new data should enable scientists to tackle myriad long-standing questions: What is Mercury's interior made of, and where does its magnetic field come from? How was the planet formed, and to what extent is it still tectonically active today? By making precise measurements of the spacecraft's orbit and position, a radio experiment will also provide a new test of Einstein's theory of general relativity . Stay tuned for more updates from ESA about humanity's first visit to Mercury in more than a decade.
